en: The Sutra on the Original Action of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: Assembling the Multitude. Chapter One: Assembling the Multitude. First.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha again traveled to the site of the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of King Bimbisāra, where he had previously attained perfect enlightenment, and sat there as before.

When he first attained Buddhahood, his radiance was exceedingly bright; now, once more, he emitted forty-two rays of light. Each ray was adorned with a necklace of millions of asaṃkhyeya rays of merit, beautifying the Buddha’s body so that it filled the entire Dharma-realm. Serene as empty space, he concentrated his spirit to illuminate stillness; delighting in the nature of eternal abiding, he exhausted the essence of transformation through his spiritual power.

The Great Function is without method; he is the King of Dharma and Lord of Dharma, acting as father and mother to all sentient beings. Spontaneously, there are hundreds of thousands of precious lotus lion-thrones, just as those upon which the Buddhas of antiquity sat. Their virtue, moral discipline, majestic demeanor, and marks of excellence are identical; their bodies and minds are pure, and they are universally endowed with meritorious conduct.

The adamantine treasure-trove penetrated by this radiance produces infinite emanations that illuminate the lands of sentient beings; throughout the past, future, and present, there is no further obstruction. These emanations reach all beings, delivering the Dharma to people such that the three periods of time are entirely equalized; its perfect clarity and singular penetration are equal to those of all Buddhas.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas were all in their final birth before buddhahood; their spiritual powers were wondrously perfected as they pervaded the ten directions. Their dharma-bodies were infinite as they guided and benefited sentient beings, opening the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and manifesting the wondrous fruit of the Buddha-nature. These essential teachings of quiescent non-action entered the very faculties of all people.

They train and transform others through the knowledge of past lives; they enter the boundless through a gradual mind; they understand that the essentials of the internal and external are from beginning to end infinite; and they regard all Buddha-lands as equal, without making any distinctions.

With mouths of great compassion, they extol the names of the Buddhas beyond measure; there is nothing among the affairs of the six realms that they do not penetrate and understand. Wherever they transform beings, everyone reaches the point of exclaiming in praise:
"The Buddha has mindful regard for us and established our great resolve, thereby manifesting to us all the various lands—both good and evil, superior and inferior—within the worlds of all Buddhas."
The Buddha dwells and resides wherever he pleases, propagating and exalting his guidance and transformation; with his radiant supernormal powers, he instructs us and reveals our own intent.

Regarding the *Buddha-mūla-karma-avataṃsaka*—the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, the Stainless Stage, and the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment—the Buddha has explained their essentials for me, severing my flaws as well as all doubts and delusions, and has fully manifested for me the Buddha-lands, the Buddha-body, the Buddha’s spiritual powers, the Buddha’s strengths, and the Buddha’s meditative concentrations.

With immeasurable transformations, the four immeasurables, the fearlessnesses, the three types of faultless karma, and the eighteen unique qualities, he extensively expounds the teachings on all merits and the dharmas of the unsurpassed path, which flow into all lands throughout the ten directions.
"To the east, at the limitlessness of space, lies the realm of Fragrant Forest; the Buddha there is named Entering Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Reverent Head.
To the south, at the limitlessness of space, lies the realm of Joyful Forest; the Buddha there is named Not Forsaking Joy, and the Bodhisattva is named Awakening Head."
To the west, at an infinite distance, lies the Flower Forest Land; its Buddha is named Practice of Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Jewel Head.
To the north, at an infinite distance, lies the Path Forest Land; its Buddha is named Practice of Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Wisdom Head.
To the northeast, at the limitlessness of space, there is the Blue Lotus Land; the Buddha’s name is Compassionate Diligence, and the Bodhisattva’s name is Virtue Chief.
To the southeast, at the limitlessness of space, there is the Golden Forest Land; the Buddha’s name is Exhaustive Diligence, and the Bodhisattva’s name is Eye Chief.
To the southwest, at the infinite distance, lies the Jewel Forest Land; the Buddha there is named Supreme Diligence, and the Bodhisattva is named Bright Head.
To the northwest, at the infinite distance, lies the Vajra Land; the Buddha there is named Deliverance by the Single Vehicle, and the Bodhisattva is named Dharma Head.
Below, at the limitlessness of space, there is a crystal buddha-field; the Buddha’s name is Great Diligence, and the bodhisattva’s name is Wisdom Chief.
Above, at the limitlessness of space, there is a forest-of-desire buddha-field; the Buddha’s name is Ultimate Diligence, and the bodhisattva’s name is Worthy Chief.
In this way, the light of all dharmas flowed in and pervaded everywhere without exception.

At that time, the Muni Buddha praised the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, saying that they were all the foremost in their respective lands, and that each had come to this great assembly together with countless superior beings.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat upon thrones of lotuses made of a thousand jewels.
At that time, the foremost bodhisattva among the assembly in that land, named Gīrśa, by the power of the Buddha’s sanctity, uttered this praise:

"How wonderful is the gathering of this assembly! Behold the purity of the Buddha-land where they dwell, from their Dharma robes and the virtuous conduct of the Tathāgata, to the causes of the forty-two ranks of sages. They expound the sutras and dharmas to attain the transformative powers of a Buddha; according to the clarity or turbidity of each realm, they deliver beings boundlessly, spreading the transformative influence of the Way so that it reaches everywhere."

Thus, in the Buddha-lands of other directions, the *Necklace of Fundamental Practice* (*Yingluo benye*) is likewise taught as non-dual and undifferentiated; the Dharma of the path revealed therein is no different from that which Śākyamuni now teaches.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Reverent Head, entering into the spiritual powers of all Buddhas across the lands of the ten directions and uttering the Great Lion’s Roar, inquired after the Dharma-gate of the Vajra Necklace, the ocean-like treasury of immeasurable jewels of all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.

At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha first arrived beneath the tree, he observed the manifestations of the faculties and conditions of sentient beings throughout the dharma realms of the ten directions; he then emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entirety of the buddha-fields, causing those from as high as the four formless heavens to descend simultaneously into the dharma assembly.
The eighteen heavens, the six heavens, and the four heavens all assembled.

From immeasurable lands—each land consisting of a single Mount Sumeru surrounded by the sun and moon that illuminate the four continents: Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north.
The boundaries of the kingdom are encircled by an iron wall surrounding a great ocean, above which are the twenty-eight heavens; such is one small kingdom.
Encompassing the ten directions, there are a total of ten billion such lands.
At that time, the Buddha’s radiance manifested entirely within them. Furthermore, there were the Four Heavenly Kings;

the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and the gods of the Brahmā realms: the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Akaniṣṭha, Ākāśānantyāyatana, Vijñānānantyāyatana, Ākiṃcanyāyatana, and Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana. All such devas possess great pools of water from which lotus flowers grow; therefore, they are called Water Devas (Āpsarā).
The four classes of non-material sentient beings are all born by transformation.
Reaching down to the limits of the five wheels,
this constitutes a single Buddha-field, named the Dharma-realm of Great Patience.

The hundred billion emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha pervaded all within it, preaching for those in that land the practices of the *adornment* (*mālā*) of the fundamental karma of the worthy and holy ones.

At that time, the great assembly of devas and humans perceived the Buddha and the bodhisattvas of that small land as if they were meeting face-to-face nearby, and they all came together to this assembly under the tree at the Vajra-Silent-Nirvana Dharma-Ground.

Chapter Two: Names of the Worthies and Sages The *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-mūla-karman-sūtra*, Chapter Two: Names of the Worthies and Sages. At that time, the Bodhisattva Respectful Head from another direction, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, and because the great assembly consisted entirely of dragon kings, lion kings, and the twenty-eight heavenly kings—all of whom possessed great roots and great practices and had received the Buddha’s supernatural powers—put forward a small inquiry.
He asked the Buddha: "Great Teacher!..."

By what practice did you originally cultivate the holy path to Buddhahood? Your body, speech, and mind are pure, indestructible like a vajra; no sentient being can find fault in them, for your inner nature is luminously radiant, eternally abiding and never ceasing.

Surpassing all bodhisattvas, he gives birth to a countenance of unsurpassed beauty and symmetry; perfectly complete, spontaneous, unconditioned, and pure, his two kinds of eternal bodies deliver immeasurable beings.

Manifesting within the six realms of existence, he is constantly revered by Śakra and Brahmā; he dispels darkness like a candle flame, illuminates heaven and earth like the sun and moon, and ferries devas and humans like a boatman. Transcending the three realms, he stands as the Honored One of Wondrous Enlightenment.
"If one wishes to accomplish this path, how should one practice?
What are the names of all the worthy ones and sages?
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Saṃcodaka with his adamantine voice, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well and practice in accordance with the Dharma.

Previously, among the devas and humans, I extensively expounded all the infinite practices and vows of the Bodhisattvas. This Dharma is also that which has been joyfully proclaimed by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—the definitive, ultimate *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli) necklace of the path traversed by the Buddhas.”
Now, for the sake of this great assembly—the faculties of all fourteen nayutas of people—I shall reveal the *Necklace of Fundamental Karma*.

You should keep this in mind; your aspirations are lofty and far-reaching, and you transform others through supreme great compassion, extending your kindness to all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha!
Those who wish to accomplish this path should first rectify the three karmas, practice the teachings of the Three Jewels, and have faith in and orientation toward cause and effect."
However, regarding what you have asked, one may enter all the Buddha-teachings; as a bodhisattva, one will attain Buddhahood before long.

One must diligently study and learn the forty-two names of the worthy sages (*ārya*), which constitute the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time speak this in common, as one and not two.
“O Son of the Buddha! These are:
*yogācāra*, which in the language of Qin means ‘Abiding in the Generation of the Resolve’; *yogakṣema*, which in the language of Qin means ‘Abiding in the Cultivation of the Ground’;
*yogakara*, which in the language of Qin means ‘Abiding in Practice’; *yogamātra*, which in the language of Qin means ‘Abiding in Noble Birth’; and *praśrabdhi*...”
*Prayoga* (婆沙) means "Abiding in the Perfection of Skillful Means" (*Upāyakauśalyasampannavihāra*) in the language of Qin; *Vivarti* (毘跋致) means "Abiding in the Rectified Mind" (*Sūcittavihāra*);
*Avivarti* (阿毘跋致) means "Abiding in Non-retrogression" (*Avinivartanīyavihāra*); *Bikṣaka* (必叉伽) means "Abiding in the Youthful" (*Kumārabhūtavihāra*);
*Bhadrakalpa* (必阿羅) means "Abiding as a Prince of the Dharma" (*Dharmarājaputravihāra*); *Rājyābhiṣeka* (留止迦) means "Abiding in the Consecration" (*Abhiṣekavihāra*); *Dugā* (度伽阿).
The Chinese term for *pramuditā* is "practice of joy"; the Chinese term for *vimalā* is "practice of benefit";
the Chinese term for *prabhākārī* is "practice of freedom from anger and resentment"; the Chinese term for *arciṣmatī* is "practice of inexhaustibility";

the Chinese term for *sudurjayā* is "practice of being free from delusion and confusion"; the Chinese term for *abhimukhī* is "practice of good manifestation"; the Chinese term for *dūraṃgamā* is "practice of the far-reaching."
*Adhiṣṭhāna-caryā* (Aḥqín yán: practice of respect); *Buddha-ka* (Aḥqín yán: practice of wholesome dharmas); *Dharmākhyāna-pada* (Aṇqín yán: practice of truth);
*Sarvasattva-trāṇa-pariṇāmanā* (Luódi liúshā yán: dedication for the protection and rescue of all sentient beings);
*Akṣaya-pariṇāmanā* (Luótánshā yán: indestructible dedication); *Vimala-garbha* (Bìbáijiā yán).
"Equal to all Buddhas" dedication; "Dharma-bhiṣa" (in the language of Qin, *zhì yīqièchù*) dedication, meaning "reaching all places";

"Buddhadatta" (in the language of Qin, *wújìn gōngdé zàng*) dedication, meaning "inexhaustible treasury of merit"; "Rakṣabhiṣa" (in the language of Qin, *suíshùn píngděng shàngēn*) dedication, meaning "dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality";
and "Śilākṣaga" (in the language of Qin, *suíshùn děngguān yīqiè zhòngshēng*) dedication, meaning "dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings."
The dedication of birth; the dedication of *bhūtakoṭi* (translated in the Qin language as "the mark of reality");

the dedication of *pratimokṣa* (translated in the Qin language as "unfettered liberation"); the dedication of *dharmadhātu-apramāṇa* (translated in the Qin language as "the immeasurable realm of phenomena");
the *kumārabhūmi* (translated in the Qin language as "the stage of joy that flows against the current"); and the *sukha-eka* (translated in the Qin language as...).
The Path of Vaidūrya, the Ground Free from Defilement; Sunāga, which in the Qin language means the Ground of Flowing Illumination;
Srotāpanna, which in the Qin language means the Ground of Observing the Radiance of Wisdom; Sakṛdāgāmin, which in the Qin language means the Ground of Crossing Obstacles and Difficulties;

Anāgāmin, which in the Qin language means the Ground of the Thinning of Outflows and Manifestation; and Arhat, which in the Qin language means the Ground of Transcending the Three Existences and Far-reaching Travel.
Aniruddha (A-ni-luo-han) means "Transformation-Birth Immovable Ground" in the language of Qin; Anāgha (A-na-he) means "Wisdom-Light Sublime-Goodness Ground" in the language of Qin;
Arhat (A-he-lo-fu) means "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct Dharma-Cloud Ground" in the language of Qin;
Mahāikaṣāya (Mo-he-yi-huo-sha) means "Signless Stainless Ground" in the language of Qin; Saghabhagavabuddha (Sa-qie-po-jia-po-fo-tuo) means... in the language of Qin.
The Wondrous Enlightenment is the Unsurpassed Ground.
"O Son of the Buddha!

For this reason, these gates of names encompass all meritorious practices; neither Buddhas nor Bodhisattvas fail to enter these gates of names. All spiritual powers, all causes and effects, and all realms likewise enter these gates of names."
O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the gate through which the path taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions is identical—neither increasing nor decreasing—a definitive lion’s roar.

You should make this vow to yourself: to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning and flavor, and to pray that all sentient beings may together enter my Dharma and become equal to me as Buddhas.
"You should train yourselves in this way.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Foremost Reverence:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
I shall now briefly explain one noble lineage among the noble lineages, namely, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).

Prior to ascending this stage, there are ten stages of conforming to names; therein, the Bodhisattva constantly practices ten mentalities, namely: the mentality of faith, the mentality of mindfulness, the mentality of diligence, the mentality of wisdom, the mentality of concentration, the mentality of non-retrogression, the mentality of dedication, the mentality of protection, the mentality of precepts, and the mentality of vows.
O Son of the Buddha!
If one practices this mind for one kalpa, two kalpas, or three kalpas, one will then attain entry into the stage of the First Abode.
Dwelling in this stage, one further cultivates the hundred dharma-gates of clarity, namely, the ten levels of faith.
Since there are ten aspects of mind within each moment of mind, one practices the "Dharma-gate of the Hundred Dharmas of Clarity.
One constantly generates immeasurable great vows of both active practice and non-practice, and within the stage of the Human Nature and the Seed-Nature, one extensively fulfills all such vows.
“Having set out as a worthy one, I have made vast vows; from this life until reaching Buddhahood, may all vows be fulfilled.
Within my vows, there is nothing that shall not be accomplished; having personally attained Buddhahood, my original vows shall be the foundation.”
As I now practice giving, I vow that all sentient beings shall abandon the mind of greed and enter the stage of the path of emptiness.
As I constantly practice the Dharma-precepts, I vow that all sentient beings shall maintain their conduct without violation and attain true liberation.
Constantly upholding the six patiences, may all beings attain a mind free from contention and abide in the patience of the dharma of tranquility.
Possessing the power of great diligence, may all beings practice without ceasing and enter the fruit of self-awakening.
Abiding in a mind of meditative concentration, may all beings be fully endowed with supernormal powers and dwell in peace through the unconditioned.
Cultivating the wisdom of the True Dharma, may all beings enter the flow of the ocean of insight and succeed to the rank of Bodhisattvas.
Practicing the vow of signlessness, one should wish that all sentient beings may have all their vows fulfilled and flow into the ocean of the Buddhas.
With great wisdom and skillful means, one should wish that all sentient beings may have unimpeded rivers of Dharma and reach the limit of the two truths.
With great power and supernormal faculties, may all beings have transformations at their command and attain fearlessness.
With the perfection of ultimate wisdom, may all beings perfect vajra-wisdom and ascend to the fruit of the site of enlightenment.
Entering the Stainless Ground (Vimalā-bhūmi), may all beings sit beneath the Bodhi tree and transform all sentient beings.
Having now attained awakening, may all beings understand the conventional nature of continuity and extinguish the mind that clings to nihilism.

When awakening to and illuminating the transformation of dharmas, one should wish that all sentient beings realize that phenomena are formed through conditions and extinguish the mind that clings to permanence.
When attaining the fulfillment of the body, one should wish that all sentient beings realize the dharma of mutual dependence and extinguish the mind that clings to a self.
With objectless great compassion, may all beings understand that things arise from false causes and extinguish the mind of views and attachments.
With the foremost nirvana, may all beings awaken to the conditions of the true Dharma and extinguish the mind of attachment to precepts.
Attaining the fruit of the ten powers, may all beings awaken to the illumination of the two truths and extinguish the mind of false views. With the power of the vajra,
may all beings awaken to the twelve links of dependent origination and extinguish the mind of doubt and wrong views.
Shining alone and without limit, may all sentient beings recognize that dharmas are impermanent and extinguish their hearts of greed and stinginess.
Possessing the five eyes and the three penetrations, may all sentient beings cultivate the awakening of the three insights and extinguish their hearts of delusion and darkness.
In unimpeded harmony, may all beings inherit the understanding of the Triple Gem and extinguish hearts of anger and contention.
Attaining great, luminous wisdom, may all beings enter into all emptiness and extinguish the storehouse of ignorance.
With the thirty-two marks, may all beings have each mark adorned and excellent, extinguishing the fruits of dependent retribution;
may they attain the function of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya). May all beings board the great Dharma-ship and enter the ocean of the Buddha-Dharma.
My vows regarding cause and effect are all fully perfected; all practices and vows are subsumed therein.
These twenty-four vows encompass immeasurable practices; they take faith and aspiration as their initial gateway and ultimate wisdom as their foundation.
Now, before all the Buddhas, I received the great vows; those vows are now fulfilled, and I shall cultivate and advance in further practices.
As for the merit therein, even if practiced for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I vow to relinquish it and enter the immeasurable realms.
"All Bodhisattvas, if they enter this vow, there are none who do not gain entry into the ocean of sarvajñā.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Having dwelt in this stage and made these great vows, one transcends all external ordinary beings who practice the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

Now, one further cultivates immeasurable merits, namely the ten *pāramitās*, the three gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—and the emptiness of existence and non-existence. Upon achieving the contemplation of emptiness, one eliminates the notions of self, person, agent, and sentient being; gradually abandoning all views, the bonds of the triple world, and the [false conceptions of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity, one gradually shatters ignorance and subdues and severs all karmic habits.

I shall thickly accumulate all wholesome dharmas—the eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitās*—and gather all dharma-gates within my mind, so that they do not depart from my thoughts for even a single moment.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten precepts that are not to be transgressed, which should be received and upheld.
First, do not kill humans, nor even beings up to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the twenty-eighth heaven.”
2. Not stealing, even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf.
3. Not engaging in sexual misconduct, even with non-human beings.
4. Not speaking falsely, even concerning non-human beings.
5. Not to speak of the faults and transgressions of bodhisattvas, whether they be monastics or householders;
6. Not to sell alcohol;
7. Not to praise oneself and disparage others.
8. Not being stingy.
9. Not being angry, even toward non-humans.
10. Not slandering the Triple Gem.
If one violates the ten precepts, it cannot be rectified through repentance and one enters the state of *pārājika*.
Within a single day of ten eons, one undergoes eighty-four thousand punishments and extinguishes eighty-four thousand lifetimes; therefore, they must not be violated.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
By losing this [precept], one loses everything from the Stage of Generating the Resolve, through the second and third stages, up to the tenth stage.
For this reason, this precept is the root of the practice of all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.
If all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas were to attain the fruits of the noble ones without relying on these ten gates of precepts, such a thing would be impossible.

This is the first person within the lineage of the cultivated seeds (*śikṣā-bīja*) at the stage of the first dwelling; in this manner, the Dharma-practice of the nine subsequent persons gradually expands, extending through the ninth dwelling, the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the Immaculate Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), wherein inconceivable conduct likewise gradually increases and expands.
"O Son of the Buddha!
I have now briefly explained this, like a single drop from the ocean.
**Chapter Three: The Holy Ones’ Study of Contemplation** *The Sutra on the Original Action of the Bodhisattva’s Diadem* At that time, the Bodhisattva Reverent Head addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should a bodhisattva train in contemplating the meaning and characteristics of names?
Furthermore, how should they practice regarding the phenomena that the mind engages with?
The Buddha said:
“O Son of the Buddha!

Your question is identical to that which all Buddhas throughout the lands of the ten directions ask when they sit at the site of enlightenment; it is none other than the question asked by Saṃdarśana.”
Listen attentively, listen attentively! Contemplate and observe correctly, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!
All Buddhas have taught the three gates of samādhi known as the Six Blazing Flames; I likewise teach them in this way.

The sixfold nature is the jeweled necklace of all bodhisattvas' merits, which adorns and sustains the two kinds of dharma-bodies of bodhisattvas; it is the necklace of the millions of *asaṃkhyeya* meritorious practices worn by bodhisattvas.
If all Bodhisattvas were to enter the stage of right determination without entering the gateway of the merit of the *ratna-āvalī* (necklace/adornment), such a thing is impossible.
"O Son of the Buddha!

As for 'nature' (*gotra*), it refers to the nature of the stage of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*), the nature of the innate stage (*prakṛti-gotra*), the nature of the stage of the path (*mārga-gotra*), the nature of the noble stage (*ārya-gotra*), the nature of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-gotra*), and the nature of wondrous enlightenment (*vicitra-bodhi-gotra*)."
They are also called the six firmnesses; they are likewise called firm faith, firm dharma, firm cultivation, firm virtue, firm summit, and firm awakening.

It is also called the six patiences: the patience of faith, the patience of dharma, the patience of cultivation, the patience of correctness, the stainless patience, and the patience of all-knowledge.

It is also called the six wisdoms: the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, the wisdom of cultivation, the wisdom of signlessness, the wisdom of illuminating quiescence, and the wisdom of quiescent illumination.

It is also called the six concentrations: the concentration on the cultivation of signs, the concentration on nature, the concentration on the wisdom of the path, the concentration on the wisdom of the aspects of the path, the concentration on great wisdom, and the concentration on correct contemplation.

It is also called the six contemplations: the contemplation of abiding, the contemplation of practice, the contemplation of heading toward, the contemplation of the stages, the contemplation of signlessness, and the contemplation of the knowledge of all modes.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There is not a single Bodhisattva or Buddha who does not enter this Dharma-gate of the definitive true reality of the six kinds of clear contemplation.
O Son of the Buddha!"

Regarding what you previously mentioned concerning names—namely, the name "Bodhisattva" as applied to the copper-jewel necklace—it refers to the ten individuals within the stage of the nature of practice (*śikṣāgotra*). Their names are: the Bodhisattva dwelling in the generation of the mind (*cittotpādavihāra*), the Bodhisattva purifying the ground (*bhūmipariśodhana*), the Bodhisattva practicing cultivation (*pratipatti*), the Bodhisattva born into nobility (*janmakula*), the Bodhisattva perfected in skillful means (*upāyaparigṛhīta*), the Bodhisattva of right mind (*samyakcitta*), the Bodhisattva non-retrogressive (*avinivartanīya*), the Bodhisattva of youthful truth (*kumārabhūta*), the Bodhisattva son of the Dharma-king (*dharmarājaputra*), and the Bodhisattva consecrated with empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
“O Son of the Buddha!

Regarding the designation ‘Bodhisattva Adorned with Silver Jewel Necklaces,’ there are ten individuals within the nature-born lineage (*gotra*), whose names are: the Bodhisattva Joyful, the Bodhisattva Beneficial, the Bodhisattva Free from Resentment, the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible, the Bodhisattva Free from Delusion and Confusion, the Bodhisattva Well-Appearing, the Bodhisattva Unattached, the Bodhisattva Honorable, the Bodhisattva Virtuous Dharma, and the Bodhisattva Truth.”
“O Son of the Buddha!

Regarding the designation ‘Bodhisattva Adorned with Gold and Jewel Necklaces,’ there are ten persons within the stage of the lineage of the nature of the Way (*mārgajātīya*), whose names are: the Bodhisattva Who Protects All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings, the Indestructible Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Equal to All Buddhas, the Bodhisattva Reaching All Places, the Bodhisattva Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit, the Bodhisattva of Equal Roots of Goodness, the Bodhisattva Who Contemplates Sentient Beings in Accordance with Reality, the Bodhisattva of Suchness, the Bodhisattva Unbound and Liberated, and the Bodhisattva of the Infinite Dharma Realm.”
“O Son of the Buddha!

Regarding the bodhisattvas designated by the name ‘Vaidūrya Jewel Garland,’ there are ten persons within the noble lineage; their names are: the Bodhisattva Joyful, the Bodhisattva Free from Defilement, the Bodhisattva Radiant Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Blazing Light, the Bodhisattva Difficult to Conquer, the Bodhisattva Manifesting Presence, the Bodhisattva Far-Going, the Bodhisattva Immovable, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Light, and the Bodhisattva Dharma Cloud.”
“O Son of the Buddha!

These one million asaṃkhyeya garlands of merit adorn and sustain the two kinds of dharma-bodies of Bodhisattvas. These forty persons are called those who practice learning; they enter the stream of the Dharma to pour it upon themselves.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Regarding the name ‘Bodhisattva Maṇiratna-hāra,’ among those of the nature of Equal Enlightenment, there is one individual named Bodhisattva Vajramati-dhvaja.”

Abiding in the samādhi of the summit of tranquility, he dwells for a hundred kalpas through the power of his great vows; having cultivated a thousand samādhis, he enters the vajra-samādhi, which is identical to the nature of all phenomena—the two truths as one truth, a single unified characteristic.

Furthermore, dwelling for a thousand kalpas, he trained in the majestic deportment of the Buddha—gazing like an elephant king and walking with the stride of a lion—and further cultivated the Buddha’s immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas of supernatural powers for the purpose of transforming and guiding beings.
Therefore, all Buddha-dharmas manifest before them; they enter the sphere of the Buddhas' conduct, sit upon the terrace of enlightenment, and transcend the three māras.

Furthermore, they dwell for ten thousand kalpas, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood, entering the Great Samādhi of Quiescence, and awakening equally with all Buddhas. Beyond the realm of the two truths, they are neither existent nor non-existent, without mind and without form; as for the two habitual tendencies of cause and effect, none remain.
He manifests as identical to the Buddhas of antiquity, possessing only responsive names; he manifests various forms and minds to teach and transform sentient beings.

He manifests as identical to the Buddhas of old, constantly practicing the Middle Way; yet while great bliss and non-action differ from arising and ceasing, he is in reality not a Buddha, for he manifests the supernatural powers of a Buddha while eternally abiding in his original realm.

“O Son of the Buddha! A crystal necklace is transparent and radiant both inside and out; likewise, the wondrous nature of constant awakening is profoundly still, luminous, and pure, and is named the Ground of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

It eternally abides in the Middle Way above all dharmas, transcending the four māras. It is neither existent nor non-existent, as all marks have been exhausted. One suddenly realizes the Great Awakening, exhausting the spiritual essence of transformation; the two bodies abide eternally to transform those with whom there is a karmic affinity.”
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
I shall now briefly state the names of the worthy and noble ones; you should receive, uphold, and put them into practice to transform others.
"O Son of the Buddha! [he continued].
Regarding what you previously asked about the dharmas upon which the mind operates,
they are the so-called ten minds:
first, the stage of generating the resolve;...
2. Abiding in the mind that purifies the ground;
3. Abiding in the mind of practice;
4. Abiding in the mind of noble birth;
5. Dwelling in the Mind of Expedient Means;
6. Dwelling in the Right Mind;
7. Dwelling in the Non-regressing Mind;
8. Abiding in the mind of a youthful prince;
9. Abiding in the mind of a Dharma Prince;
10. Abiding in the mind of consecration.
"Furthermore, the dharmas to be contemplated by means of the ten contemplations of the mind are as follows:

First, the thick accumulation of all roots of goodness, namely the Four Great Vows: to cause those who have not yet crossed over the Truth of Suffering to cross over the Truth of Suffering; to cause those who have not yet understood the Truth of Origination to understand the Truth of Origination; to cause those who have not yet been established in the Truth of the Path to be established in the Truth of the Path; and to cause those who have not yet attained Nirvana to attain Nirvana."
“O Son of the Buddha!
Second, one cultivates immeasurable wholesome practices, namely the four foundations of mindfulness: contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
If these four are all empty, then the four inversions will not exist.”
One does not destroy conventional designations because all dharmas are such.

That they are all like illusions and transformations means that the five aggregates—form, consciousness, sensation, perception, and formations—the six elements including consciousness and space, the four great elements, and all dharmas, have neither self-characteristics nor other-characteristics, for they are like empty space.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Third, one skillfully practices the Dharma of the Buddha-way, which is known as contemplating the ten universal bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*):
the four great elements, the four colors, the sphere of space, and the sphere of consciousness, all because they are in accordance with the true mark of reality (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*).”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Fourth, one receives the Dharma and practices it in the presence of all Buddhas; that is to say, the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*):

two bases of mastery consisting of the broad and concise aspects within the actual five aggregates internally; two bases of mastery consisting of the broad and concise aspects among the provisional phenomena of sentient beings externally; and four bases of mastery consisting of the broad and concise aspects of the four great elements.
Thus one contemplates all phenomena as empty because they are signless.
"O Son of the Buddha!
There are five practices of all pure and white dharmas, namely, the eight awakenings of the great person (aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ):"
Having few desires, contentment, tranquility, diligence, right mindfulness, right concentration, right wisdom, and non-contentiousness, because they accord with all dharmas.
“O Son of the Buddha!
The sixth is being protected by all Buddhas, namely the contemplation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*):

through the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), one realizes that the two marks of internal and external designations (*prajñapti*) are unattainable; this is the first liberation, which is the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).”
Because the five internal dharmas and all external dharmas are unapprehendable, there is the wisdom of cultivation regarding the second liberation.

Because the five aggregates of the form realm are fully observed as empty, and because the third liberation, the four emptinesses, the five aggregates, and the contemplation of the meditative attainment of cessation are all unapprehendable, [there is the wisdom of cultivation regarding the third liberation].
Because the five liberations are identical to suchness.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Seventh, the extensive propagation of the True Dharma, namely the six points of harmonious respect:

"Their three karmas are identical in precepts, identical in views, and identical in practice; they enter together into this Dharma-harmony because it is ultimately empty and because they abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
O Son of the Buddha!"
Eighth, having faith and joy in the Great Dharma, which refers to the three emptinesses:

because all causes are empty, there is no volitional action; because all effects are empty, there is no mark; and because both the emptiness of cause and the emptiness of effect are further empty, it is the emptiness of emptiness.
Such dharmas are like space. "O Son of the Buddha! Ninth, the mind abides in the fourfold equal dharmas:

namely, transforming sentient beings by teaching the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; that the three realms are not pleasure but suffering; that birth is endless due to the habitual causes of ignorance; and that the path-factors of the three emptinesses lead to unconditioned quiescence."
The Four Truths are non-dual, for they are of a single unified character.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Tenth, one should earnestly seek the merits of the Buddha, namely, the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti):"
The Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, renunciation, and the devas—by these one attains all the merits of the Buddhas.
In every thought-moment, one enters the non-illusory samādhi, because what is constantly practiced is manifested before one through cultivation.
O Son of the Buddha!
Previously, while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, I spoke of the names of the Ten Contemplations; these are the practices of ordinary beings in the first ten stages of abiding (*bhūmi*).
If there are any Bodhisattvas, none fail to enter this gate and head toward the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
“O Son of the Buddha!
As for the mind of the ten practices: first, the practice of the joyful mind;
second, the practice of the beneficial mind;”
3. Practice with a mind free from ill will;
4. Practice with an inexhaustible mind;
5. Practice with a mind free from delusion and confusion.
Sixth, the practice of a virtuous mind;
seventh, the practice of an unattached mind;
eighth, the practice of a respectful mind.
9. The mental activity of wholesome dharmas;
10. The mental activity of reality.
Furthermore, regarding the ten objects of contemplation for the contemplation of the mind: first, it is for the sake of personally attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
These are the four right dharmas:

employing skillful means to cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise; employing skillful means to cause arisen wholesome dharmas to increase and expand; employing skillful means to prevent unarisen unwholesome dharmas from arising; and employing skillful means to abandon arisen unwholesome dharmas.
At that time, the bodhisattva acts for the sake of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Second, it is for the sake of attaining great power within one's own body."
The so-called four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are:
mindfulness guarding the object, diligence striving toward it, concentration restraining and gathering it, and wisdom illuminating the object.
This is because one attains the non-arising of phenomena and mastery over them.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Third, because they are fully endowed with fearlessness through their vows.
These are the five faculties (pañcendriya):”
Faith, mindfulness, diligence, concentration, and wisdom are all without marks.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Fourth, it is because of seeking the fulfillment of the Three Jewels."
This refers to the fivefold Dharma-body: morality eliminates physical transgressions;

concentration ensures the mind is not distracted; wisdom awakens one to the emptiness of perceptions; liberation is free from all burdens; and through this burdenless state, one perceives that all sentient beings are without bondage.
It is for the sake of knowledge, vision, and liberation, because all phenomena are empty and non-dual.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Fifth, it is for the sake of transforming all sentient beings."
What is called the Eightfold Noble Path:
from the teacher, one gives rise to wisdom, which is termed Right View;
from the Dharma, one gives rise to reflection, which is termed Right Thought.
Exerting oneself without weariness is called right effort;
leaving the household life to receive the Way and attaining the factors conducive to the threefold path is called right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
entering the emptiness of the nature of phenomena is called right concentration and right wisdom.
Because they contemplate non-arising and non-duality as a single unified whole.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Sixth, because they have attained great compassion."
What are called the seven contemplations are:

the contemplation of the dharma of discernment, the dharma of mindfulness, the dharma of diligence, the dharma of protection, the dharma of joy, the dharma of concentration, and the dharma of wisdom. These are termed the gate of contemplation because they enter into the single characteristic.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Seventh, it is for the sake of attaining the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
These are the five roots of goodness:”

It is the contemplation of correct observation, the contemplation of warmth, the contemplation of the summit, the contemplation of patience, and the supreme contemplation of the emptiness of the three realms; for it can give rise to the great wisdom of signlessness of the ten stages, because it is the unchanging embryo of the sages and because it is the equality of the supreme emptiness.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Eighth, because of entering and practicing within all Buddha-lands.
This refers to the four methods of transformation:”

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
These four are of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*), for they illuminate that all phenomena are unarisen and enter into practice within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
“O Son of the Buddha!
The ninth is because one illuminates all phenomena within a single thought-moment.
That is to say, the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time:”
In the past, there are two: ignorance and volitional formations.
In the present, there are consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming.
The future arises and ceases;
all are formed through provisional conjunction, for their essential nature cannot be found.
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
Tenth, for the sake of freely turning the Great Wheel of Dharma.
This refers to the Three Jewels of the Bodhisattva:
at that time, within the Middle Way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), wisdom constitutes the Jewel of Awakening (*bodhi-ratna*).
Since all dharmas are without arising or movement, they function as the Dharma Jewel.
Constantly traversing the six realms and harmonizing with the sentient beings therein is called the Sangha Jewel.
It turns all sentient beings so that they flow into the ocean of Buddhahood.
"O Son of the Buddha!
In the Yāma Heaven, I preached the ten practices of ordinary beings for the sake of the devas."
Now, within this assembly, I shall briefly expound the essentials of the Dharma; you should receive and uphold them, for all Buddhas likewise speak thus:
"O Son of the Buddha!
As for the ten minds of dedication: first, the mind of dedication that rescues and protects all sentient beings while remaining free from signs."
2. The mind of dedication that is indestructible;
3. The mind of dedication equal to all Buddhas;
4. The mind of dedication that reaches all places;
Fifth, the mind of dedication that is an inexhaustible treasury of merit;
sixth, the mind of dedication that accords with roots of goodness that are equal;
seventh, the mind of dedication that accords with the impartial observation of all sentient beings;
8. The mind of dedication according to the nature of reality;
9. The mind of dedication of liberation without bondage;
10. The mind of dedication to the immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
"Furthermore, regarding the ten contemplations on the mind as the objects of observation: first, the straightforwardness of the two truths.
This refers to studying the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), observing that the characteristics of all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*) and are ultimately ungraspable."

Through the teachings of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they instruct the six classes of heavenly beings; with shaven heads and clad in the robes of the Triple Gem, these renunciant bodhisattvas join the entire Saṃgha, for there is no duality in the Buddha-dharma and it is supremely pure.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Second is the wisdom of the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This refers to the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):”
This is the functional differentiation of the nature of wisdom; therefore, the celestial mind is called "divine" (*deva*), and by means of this, the celestial body possesses supernormal powers.
With the divine eye, one perceives all phenomena throughout the three periods of time, seeing even subtle forms and so forth.
Through the divine ear, one hears the sounds of the ten directions;
through the divine knowledge of others' minds, one knows the minds of all people;
and through the divine knowledge of past lives, one knows the destinies and lifespans within the three periods of time and the six realms of existence.
Because one perceives all phenomena through the wisdom of non-arising.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Third, pure arrival."
This refers to the four kinds of indestructible purity within the wisdom of non-arising:
because one’s faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts is indestructible.
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
Fourth, the measure is equal to the power of a Buddha.
This refers to the three characteristics:

all phenomena are originally non-existent and are conventionally designated as arising; having existed, they return to non-existence and are conventionally designated as ceasing; and there is no empty existence of phenomena, which is conventionally designated as abiding.
Therefore, all that penetrates emptiness as non-dual is called the "emptiness of the characteristics of conventional truth," because emptiness is the single characteristic of truth.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Fifth, [the bodhisattva] skillfully evaluates the power of sentient beings."
Regarding the so-called five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*):
as for form (*rūpa*), because it is a collection of various empty forms that constitute the great division of form, the characteristic of form is empty.
Because it is constituted moment by moment by the mind, the characteristic of the mind is empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have neither accumulation nor dispersal, for they are of a single characteristic, which is the absence of characteristics.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Sixth is the power of the Buddha’s transformative teaching."
What are called the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are as follows:
when the six external objects reach the six internal faculties, they become the points of entry for consciousness; therefore, they are called "bases.
For one who observes with wisdom, [consciousness] is not within, not without, and not in between, because all phenomena are without self and without other.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Seventh is the progression toward unimpeded wisdom.
This refers to the eighteen realms (*dhātus*):”
The six objects, the six faculties, and the six consciousnesses constitute a single composite; all phenomena likewise constitute a single composite.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Eighth is the conformity with spontaneous wisdom."
What is called cause and effect: good and evil are termed causes, while suffering and pleasure are termed effects.
That from which something proceeds is the cause; that which arises therefrom is the effect.
Because they depend upon one another in their arising, they are collectively designated as cause and effect.
Because cause and effect are both empty, without arising and without ceasing, they are all of a single unified character.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Ninth, because one is able to receive the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha."
What is called the emptiness of the two truths:
because causes and conditions assemble, it is called "existence," yet this does not mean that existence is truly existent.
Because causes and conditions disperse, it is called "non-existence," yet this does not mean that existence is non-existent.
Therefore, existence and non-existence are both non-existent, for in prajñā and liberation there are no two distinct characteristics.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Tenth, by means of sovereign wisdom, one transforms all sentient beings."

What is called the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), is the wisdom of prajñā that abides in the center and perceives all phenomena as non-dual; as this wisdom of contemplation progressively enters the noble stages (ārya-bhūmi), it is termed the "semblance" contemplation of the Ultimate Truth, rather than the true contemplation of the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth.
As for this correct contemplation, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, there are three contemplative minds that enter all stages. These three contemplations are:

the contemplation of the two truths, which proceeds from conventional designations into emptiness; and the contemplation of equality, which proceeds from emptiness back into conventional designations.
These two contemplations constitute the path of skillful means.

By means of these two contemplations on emptiness, one attains entry into the contemplation of the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). With the dual illumination of the two truths, the mind and mental factors are simultaneously stilled and extinguished, and one enters the stream of Dharma of the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*), which is called the noble lineage of the Mahāsattva.
Because one practices the Middle Way within the signless dharma, there is no duality.
"O Son of the Buddha!

These thirty minds enter the faith of the One Vehicle; the causal dharmas of the One Vehicle cannot be attained through limited practice. Only after practicing extensively with a great mind for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, traversing the path of subduing and attaining patience, do they finally reach fulfillment."
"O Son of the Buddha!

As for those who regress or advance: prior to the ten stages (daśabhūmi), among all the dharmas of ordinary beings, there are those who give rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi* and who practice within the state of faith and conceptualization—sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who study and practice the Buddha-dharma. These constitute roots of goodness that are subject to regression."
"O sons of good family!

If one practices the ten stages of faith for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas and thereby attains entry into the ten abodes, then at that time, from the first abode through the sixth abode, if the correct contemplation of the sixth *prajñāpāramitā* manifests before them, and they further encounter the protection of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends, they will emerge into the seventh abode and abide there permanently without regression."
From this point until the seventh stage, it is called the "stage of regression.
"O Son of the Buddha!

If one does not regress, one enters the sixth stage of the practice of Prajñā; regarding emptiness, non-self, and the absence of a person or a master, there is ultimately no arising, and one will certainly enter the state of certainty."
O Son of the Buddha!
If one does not encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), one may regress from the bodhicitta for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas.

For example, among the assembly at my first gathering, eighty thousand people regressed; likewise, such as the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra, Prince Dharmamati, Śāriputra, and others, who were about to enter the seventh stage, encountered adverse conditions and consequently regressed into the unwholesome and evil states of ordinary worldlings. They were no longer called persons of the nature of the "cultivated seed" (śikṣā-bīja-gotra) and regressed into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

Whether for one kalpa, ten kalpas, or even a thousand kalpas, if one commits great false views and the five heinous crimes, performing every kind of evil without exception, this is a sign of regression.
O Son of the Buddha!

Previously, in the fourth heaven, I extensively expounded this Dharma of the ten dedications for ordinary beings; now, beneath this tree, I briefly proclaim the essentials of the teaching. You all should properly receive and practice them.
“O Son of the Buddha!
As for the mind of the ten stages: first, the four immeasurable minds;
second, the ten wholesome minds;”
3. The Mind of Luminous Radiance;
4. The Mind of Blazing Wisdom;
5. The Mind of Great Victory;
Sixth, the mind of presence;
seventh, the mind of non-arising;
eighth, the inconceivable mind;
9. The mind of the light of wisdom;
10. The mind of receiving the position.
Furthermore, regarding the ten contemplative minds and the phenomena they contemplate: first, the wisdom of the Middle Way and the Supreme Truth abiding in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

That which is called the twenty minds of joy and the ten inexhaustible vows consists in manifesting the Dharma-body to enter the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; performing the five supernormal powers and entering the Illusion-like Samādhi; manifesting the transformations of a Buddha and immeasurable merits; not receiving the temporal fruits of ordinary beings within the three realms; and constantly entering the stage of the One Vehicle, wherein one contemplates the single mind and the four truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

The two kinds of *dharmakāya* undergo transformation and rebirth; as the three contemplations manifest before them, they constantly cultivate their minds to enter the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas. This refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); because each faith contains ten aspects, there are thus a hundred dharmas of illumination. Because there are thirteen [stages], afflictions are ultimately never experienced again. With every thought extinguished within the stream of the Dharma, they naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
“O Son of the Buddha!
Second is the Dharma-treasure of the Vajra-ocean-store.

This refers to practicing the ten wholesome paths oneself and teaching others to practice the ten wholesome paths; praising those who practice the ten wholesome paths and extolling the dharma of the ten wholesome paths; manifesting in a thousand Buddha-lands to transform all sentient beings, because one has fully accomplished the signless and penetrating contemplation.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Third is the entry into the illusion-like samādhi.

This refers to the twelve gates of dhyāna, wherein the five factors of initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*) serve as the cause, while the sixth factor, the silent mind, constitutes the essence of the meditative absorption.”
With the four factors of joy, rapture, tranquility, and one-pointedness as the cause, the fifth silent mind constitutes the essence of concentration.
With the five factors of rapture, equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, and one-pointedness as the cause, the sixth silent mind constitutes the essence of concentration.

With the four factors—neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness—as its causes, these causes are termed "skillful means" (upāya); the fifth factor, the silent mind, constitutes the essence of concentration (samādhi).
"Dhyāna" (meditative absorption) is termed "branch-forest" (*aṅga-vana*), while "samādhi" (concentration) is termed "restraint and gathering.
Because it remains undispersed throughout kalpas, it is called "samādhi.
The four formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*) likewise possess five branches; because their essence and function are similar, their preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) are identical.

Regarding the "limbs" (aṅga): the five limbs—perception, protection, rightness, contemplation, and one-pointedness—act as the causes; the sixth, the silent mind, constitutes the essence of concentration (*samādhi*).

From this concentration arise the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), which are termed the "four immeasurable concentrations. This is because the Noble Ones manifest in accordance with the dharmas of ordinary beings.
“By the power of mastery, they further transcend these dharmas and enter immeasurable concentrations, in order to teach and transform all sentient beings across hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands.
O Son of the Buddha!
Fourth is the universally pervasive treasury of the Dharma Jewel.

This refers to the contemplation of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; right effort; the bases of psychic power; the faculties; the powers; the eightfold noble path; and the seven factors of enlightenment. These constitute the great practice of the Bodhisattva, for they manifest billions of Dharma-bodies to transform all sentient beings.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Fifth is the contemplation of the wisdom that enters the Dharma-realm.

This refers to the sixteen truths: the truth of existence, the truth of non-existence, the supreme truth of the middle way, the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, the truth of the path, the truth of characteristics, the truth of distinctions, the truth of viewing completion, the truth of explanation, the truth of phenomena, the truth of arising, the truth of the exhaustion of non-arising, the truth of entering the path, and the truth of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.”
The five sciences and all phenomena are entirely practiced simultaneously within a single thought-moment of the mind,
because they manifest infinite bodies in all Buddha-lands to receive the transformative influence of the Buddha-dharma.
“O Son of the Buddha!
There is a dharma called the Sixfold Pervasiveness which gives rise to wisdom by taking phenomena as its object.
This refers to the ten [aspects of] the twelve links of dependent origination and the ten kinds of illumination:”
First, the view of self as the twelve links of dependent origination;
second, the mind as the twelve links of dependent origination;
third, ignorance as the twelve links of dependent origination.
4. The twelve links of dependent origination as characteristics;
5. The twelve links of dependent origination as contributing factors;
6. The twelve links of dependent origination as the three types of karma.
7. The twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time;
8. The twelve links of dependent origination as the three types of suffering;
9. The twelve links of dependent origination as the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Tenth: By contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, one manifests immeasurable bodies; because one enters all Buddha-lands to transform all sentient beings, "O Son of the Buddha!..."
Seventh is the unobstructed and unhindered wisdom regarding the exhaustion of karmic retribution.

This means that by means of the wisdom of the three emptinesses, one contemplates the two habit-energies within the triple world; the karmic retribution of form and mind is extinguished without remainder. All activities, merits, functions, and fabrications are brought to completion; all transformations and applications, whether performed or enacted, are neither manifold nor dual, such that there is nothing in the cultivation and development that is not fully perfected.

The application of effort that develops all meritorious practices is fully perfected, and even up to the higher stages, the development of the application of effort for all meritorious practices has been completed and is entirely complete.
The roots of all conditioned phenomena are based upon the ten perfections:
giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, aspiration, skillful means, supernormal powers, and signless wisdom.

The practice of the ten pāramitās having been completed, one enters the flow of the unconditioned and uncreated Dharma, wherein every moment of mind is quiescent, naturally flowing into the ocean of sarvajñā (omniscience).
“O Son of the Buddha!
Eighth is the inconceivable effortless contemplation (*anābhoga-vipaśyanā*).

This refers to the great function of the skillful means of signless great wisdom (*animitta-mahāprajñā-upāya*), wherein the habitual tendencies of form (*rūpa-vāsanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are also exhausted. Events of a million kalpas and matters of immeasurable Buddha-lands are performed simultaneously in a single moment of mind. One manifests in the form of a Buddha and the forms of all sentient beings, performing these all at once within a single thought-moment because it is effortless.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Ninth is the wisdom that enters the limit of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*).

This refers to the complete accomplishment of all meritorious practices through the forty kinds of eloquence; the mental habituations have been extinguished and ignorance has also been removed. All Buddha-treasuries and all treasuries of transformations are practiced simultaneously within a single mind, manifesting in the forms of Buddhas and the forms of sentient beings throughout immeasurable great trichiliocosms, for the sake of teaching and transforming immeasurable sentient beings through the Dharma.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
Tenth is the contemplation of unimpeded wisdom.

This means that the rain from the immeasurable clouds of Dharma pours down upon all sentient beings; the two habitual tendencies of ignorance are now completely extinguished, and one receives the great position of office. Its spiritual transformations are immeasurable and cannot be fully described, for it manifests the same signless function as a Buddha.”
“O Son of the Buddha!
In this same way, all such worthy ones enter this gate together, practicing it until they achieve awakening.
O Son of the Buddha!”
"Previously, in the Sixth Heaven, I expounded the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to guide and transform devas and humans; now I shall briefly reveal them for you all to receive and practice.
O Son of the Buddha!
The mind of the forty-first stage is called the 'mind that enters the Dharma-realm' (*dharmadhātupraveśacitta*)."
Furthermore, as for the dharmas practiced by the mind, they are what are called the Samādhi of the Light of Dharma Entering through Valiant Subjugation.
While entering this samādhi, one practices ten dharmas:
first, training in the inconceivable transformations and adaptabilities of the Buddha;
Second, gathering the assembly of bodhisattvas;
third, again cultivating the Dharma-gates previously practiced;
fourth, visiting all Buddha-lands to inquire after the well-being of all Buddhas.
Fifth, parting from ignorance, their parents;
sixth, entering the gate of profound mystery;
seventh, manifesting in accordance with the Buddhas by assuming all manner of forms.
8. Fulfillment of the two kinds of Dharmakāya;
9. Absence of the two kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
10. Ascending to the summit of the mountain of the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Therefore, from the time he first resolved his mind upon awakening until reaching this first stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva Vimala cultivated forty minds and immeasurable dharma-gates of merit for incalculable eons. Furthermore, from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) onward, he practiced two kinds of immeasurable merits of the Dharma-body; after a hundred thousand eons, the treasury of the Dharma was finally fulfilled, whereby he entered the Samādhi of the Extinction of Marks and attained the rank of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), constantly performing the deeds of a Buddha.
"O Son of the Buddha!

Previously, within the third dhyāna, I assembled the assembly of those in the eight dhyānas and spoke one hundred trillion verses on the Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood entering the Buddha-flower Samādhi. Now, I shall briefly explain the meaning of a single verse to open the minds of sentient beings; you all should receive and uphold it."
“O Son of the Buddha!

The forty-second stage is named the Ground of the Subtle Enlightenment of the Quiescent Mind. It eternally abides in a single mark; it is the foremost and supreme, as profound and still as empty space. With all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), it illuminates and penetrates the truth of non-arising from beginning to end.”

Only the Buddha exhaustively penetrates the root of sentient beings, including their beginning and their end; the Buddha also illuminates everything down to all afflictions and the karmic retributions of all sentient beings.

With a single-minded thought, the Buddha exhaustively weighs and comprehends the origins of all things: the lands of all Buddhas, the causes and effects of all Buddhas, and the spiritual transformations of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Thus, in a single thought and at a single moment, he knows them all to abide beyond the inconceivable Two Truths, existing alone in non-duality.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Previously, while I was here beneath this tree expounding the ocean of the Dharma-realm, eighty thousand stainless Bodhisattvas manifested their bodies and attained Buddhahood.
Now, for the sake of this great assembly, I shall briefly reveal the sphere of practice for the fruit of Buddhahood; you should receive it with the highest reverence.”
The Bodhisattva Jingshou addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From the first stage to the final stage, there are two kinds of dharma-bodies: those of karmic retribution and those of spiritual transformation.”
First, the Dharma-nature body;
second, the responsive-emanation Dharma-body.
What are their physical characteristics?
"What are the characteristics of the mind?
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha!
Regarding supramundane fruits, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Buddha stage, there are two kinds of *dharmakāya* for each.
Because wisdom arises from the true nature within the stream of the *dharmadhātu* of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), this true wisdom constitutes the *dharmakāya*.
The Dharma is named "self-substance," and its accumulation constitutes the body.

Because the roots of goodness of all sentient beings evoke this Dharma-body of true wisdom, the Dharma-body is able to manifest immeasurable responsive Dharma-bodies—namely, the bodies of all realms and lands, the bodies of all sentient beings, the bodies of all Buddhas, and the bodies of all Bodhisattvas; it is able to manifest all these inconceivable bodies.
The same applies to the land.
"O Son of the Buddha!
'Land' (kṣetra) is the name for the place where all worthy sages and saints dwell."
Therefore, all sentient beings and noble sages each dwell in lands of their own karmic retribution (*vipāka*).

If ordinary sentient beings dwell within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), this constitutes the land of direct retribution; the mountains, forests, and great earth shared by them constitute the land of circumstantial retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
The noble ones of the first stage also possess two lands: first, the land of true wisdom, wherein the preceding wisdom abides as the ground for the subsequent wisdom;

second, the land of manifested transformation—whether pure or impure—which appears in accordance with the measure of kalpas, and this remains the case up to the land of the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
All sentient beings up to those on the Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi) do not abide in a pure land, as they dwell within the retribution of their karma;
only the Buddha dwells in the land of the Middle Way, the supreme Dharma-nature.
Therefore, in the past, within the Hall of Universal Radiance, I extensively expounded for all sentient beings the gateway to the Pure Land.
"O Son of the Buddha!

At the first stage (*bhūmi*), in a single thought-moment, the signless Dharma-body and Wisdom-body accomplish ten million *asaṃkhyeya* dharmas of merit, simultaneously illuminating the two truths within the stream of Dharma where every moment of mind is quiescent."

The two kinds of Dharmakāya cannot be conceived or measured by the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings, let alone by those on the second, third, or even up to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue).

However, within the realm of expedient transformation, it can be said that from the first stage (Prathamabhūmi) onward, one possesses a hundred bodies, a thousand bodies, ten thousand bodies, and even immeasurable bodies.

There is bondage and there is liberation; yet within the state of the Dharma-body, where every thought is quiescent within the flowing stream of the Dharma, one looks upward and sees no Buddha-dharmas to be sought as fruits, nor does one look downward and see any ignorance or views to be severed, nor any sentient beings to be transformed.

It is only within the context of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the teachings of skillful transformation that one perceives a Buddha who can be sought, various views that can be severed, and sentient beings who can be transformed.
Son of the Buddha!

One may also say that by practicing the three steadfast dharmas, one enters the stage of the sages; yet, within the flow of the Dharma, mind after mind is quiescent, naturally flowing into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment.
O Son of the Buddha!

Even the names of the Three Worthies and the Ten Grounds are without name and without mark; it is only for the sake of responsive transformation that the Way and Dharma of the Buddhas of antiquity possess the names of the Ten Grounds.
"O Son of the Buddha!
You should receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas as being equal and without distinction.
O Son of the Buddha!"
The worldly fruition refers to what is called the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

[In this stage, one becomes] a copper-jewel necklace-wearing copper-wheel-turning king (*tāmra-cakravartin*), with a hundred meritorious sons as his retinue; he is born in a single Buddha-field to receive the Buddha’s training and practice, and he governs two continents.

The Silver-Treasure Necklace Silver Wheel-Turning King had five hundred sons of merit as his retinue; he was born in the lands of two Buddhas to practice the Buddha’s teachings and transform the three worlds.

The Vajra-jewel-garlanded Golden Wheel-Turning King, with a thousand meritorious sons as his retinue, enters the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to transform all sentient beings while residing over the four continents.
"In the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi),

adorned with necklaces of a hundred jewels and the seven-jeweled *cakra* of the Four Heavenly Kings, with ten thousand sons as his retinue, he manifests a hundred Dharma-bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions within a hundred Buddha-fields."
The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wears a necklace of a thousand jewels and has an eight-jeweled *cakra* on his crown; he has twenty thousand sons as his retinue.
The King of the Yāma Heaven wears a necklace of ten thousand jewels and has a nine-jeweled *cakra* on his crown; his retinue is likewise beyond measure.
The Tuṣita Heaven King, adorned with necklaces of a hundred million jewels and a ten-jeweled wheel-mark, has an entourage likewise beyond measure.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven King, adorned with necklaces of celestial light jewels and an eleven-jeweled wheel-mark, has an entourage likewise.
The Heavens’ Lord of Others’ Transformations wore a necklace of mani-jewel light with twelve auspicious jewel-ribs; his retinue was likewise adorned.
The Brahma Heaven Lord wore a necklace of thousand-colored dragon-jewel light-wisdom with thirteen auspicious jewel-ribs; his retinue was likewise adorned.
The Celestial King Sound of the Great Responsive Jewel-Phase Wheel, adorned with the Brahma-Lion Jewel-Radiance Necklace, and his retinue were likewise.
The Pure Celestial King, adorned with the Inconceivable Jewel-Radiance Necklace and the White Cloud Radiance Jewel-Phase Wheel, and his retinue were likewise.

The Celestial King of Tranquil Abiding, adorned with a jeweled necklace of a million supernormal powers and radiant light, and possessing a wheel-marked jewel of fearlessness, was likewise accompanied by his retinue.

The King of the Three Realms, adorned with a jeweled necklace of a thousand celestial colors and radiant light, and possessing a wheel-marked jewel of awakened virtue, had all bodhisattvas as his retinue.
The Dharma-Realm King, whose wheel of marks of a thousand merits is adorned with the jewel-light necklace of an immeasurable treasury of merit, has Bodhisattvas in their final birth as his retinue.
O Son of the Buddha!

This upper ornament, the *cakra* (wheel) of signs, accompanies all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in their every movement and stillness, constantly following their bodies; it also transforms all sentient beings. Therefore, there exist such categories of dharmas known as "fruits of retribution."
O Son of the Buddha!

The Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness subdue the coarse karmic paths and coarse continuous fruits of the afflictions of the three realms, and they do not give rise to the coarse [afflictions] either.
This is because the Joyful Patience of the Path of Seeing subdues the karmic paths of the three realms.

The patience of detachment subdues the karmic paths of human beings; the patience of clarity subdues the karmic paths of the six heavens; the patience of flame subdues the karmic paths of various views; the patience of supremacy subdues the karmic paths of doubt and views; the patience of manifestation subdues the karmic path of causes; the patience of non-arising subdues the karmic path of results; the patience of immovability subdues the karmic path of the cause of form; the patience of light subdues the karmic path of the cause of mind; the patience of quiescence subdues the karmic path of the dual habits of mind and form; and the patience of stainlessness subdues the karmic path of the results of habituation.
The habitual tendencies of the past have already been eliminated, yet the fruit does not perish.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha!
The three stages of the Ordinary Beings (Śaikṣas) are called "subduing and abandoning through joy and patience," while from the [first] stage upward, they both subdue and abandon.
When the patience regarding the awakening to all afflictions manifests, all ignorance within the dharmadhātu is suddenly severed without remainder.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Ignorance is defined as the failure to comprehend all phenomena; it is through delusion regarding the dharmadhātu that the karmic fruits of the three realms arise."
Therefore, I say that from the storehouse of ignorance arise thirteen afflictions, namely:

false view, the view of self, the view of permanence, the view of annihilation, the view of attachment to precepts, the view of attachment to fruits, and the view of doubt—these seven views. They are called "views" because they seek after all objects.
From these views, six further attachments arise:
greed, craving, hatred, delusion, desire, and pride; they arise at all times within the dharma-realm.
"O Son of the Buddha!
All afflictions take these thirteen as their root; ignorance acts as the root for these thirteen, and thus, within the dharma-realm, they result separately in the retributions of the three realms.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Because the two karmas of seeing and attachment delude the mind regarding all forms and desires within the dharma-realm, the resulting retribution is divided into the retribution of the desire realm.
O Son of the Buddha!"

Because the two karmas of seeing and attachment delude all matter and mind within the Dharma-realm, the retribution portion arising from that matter and mind constitutes the retribution of the form realm.
"O Son of the Buddha!

Because the two karmas of view and attachment delude all concentrated minds within the dharma-realm, the retributive portion arising from those concentrated minds constitutes the retribution of the formless realm.
Therefore, within a single dharma-realm, there is the retribution of the three realms.
All conditioned phenomena—whether pertaining to ordinary beings or noble ones, whether involving views and attachments, or consisting of causes and effects—do not transcend the Dharma-realm.

Only the Buddha alone stands outside the Dharma-realm; thereafter, he returns once more to enter the treasury of the Dharma-realm, manifesting for sentient beings obscured by ignorance the infinite distinctions in the retributions of all wholesome and unwholesome paths.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Those in the preceding three stages of worthiness subdue the ignorance of the three realms, yet they still employ coarse karma. Why is this?

At the time of taking birth, with wholesome karma acting as the seed-condition and craving acting as the moisture for karma, one thus receives future fruit; therefore, while the function of [wholesome] karma ceases, the function of craving remains uninterrupted.
